units.title: Me and you
units.goal: say I, you, he, she, it and we, say yes or no, and say please and thank you.

units.title: Who I am
units.goal: say your name and where you are from.

units.title: Hello, how are you?
units.goal: say hello and goodbye, ask how someone is and say how you are.

units.title: What I want and have
units.goal: say what you would like and what you have.

units.title: My people
units.goal: talk about the people in your life.

units.title: A coffee, please
units.goal: order a drink and say who you have.

units.title: Asking questions
units.goal: ask what, who, where, when, how and why.

units.title: When I don't understand
units.goal: say you don't understand or don't know, and ask how to say something.

units.title: Can you help me?
units.goal: ask for help and say what you can, must and need.

tips.title: German always says who
tips.body: In casual English you can sometimes skip the I, but German always says who is doing something. Bin on its own is not a sentence, but ich bin means I am. That is why the cards teach the person and the verb together: ich bin, du bist, er ist. Learn each pair as one chunk, and never leave out the ich, du or er when you speak.

examples.target: Er ist Max und sie ist Lena.

tips.title: Verbs change with who does them
tips.body: In German, the verb changes a little depending on who is doing it. The ending usually tells you who: -e for ich, -st for du and -t for er or sie, so ich habe, du hast, er hat. Möchte is the odd one: ich möchte and er möchte are the same, and only du gets an ending, du möchtest. When you speak, match the verb to the person, and when you listen, the ending helps you hear who it's about.

examples.target: Sie hat Kaffee und ich habe Wasser.
examples.en: She has coffee and I have water.

examples.target: Du möchtest Kaffee, und er möchte Wasser.
examples.en: You'd like coffee, and he'd like water.

tips.title: Every noun is der, die or das
tips.body: Every German noun is masculine, feminine or neuter, and the word for the shows which one: der, die or das. This applies to people and things alike: der Vater, die Mutter, das Haus, and even das Kind. You often can't guess it, so learn every noun with its der, die or das as part of the word. If you get the word right but use the wrong der, die or das, it counts as Nearly. Every noun also starts with a capital letter, wherever it is in the sentence.

tips.title: Den and einen: the accusative
tips.body: When a der word is the thing you have, want, see or order, the little word in front of it changes, and German calls this the accusative. Der becomes den and ein becomes einen: ich habe einen Bruder, or einen Kaffee, bitte. Mein works just like ein, so my father becomes meinen Vater. Die, das, eine and plurals never change, so eine Schwester and ein Wasser stay as they are. So when you order or say who you have, check whether the noun is a der word and add the -en.

examples.target: Ich habe einen Bruder und eine Schwester.
examples.en: I have a brother and a sister.

examples.target: Einen Kaffee und ein Wasser, bitte.
examples.en: A coffee and a water, please.
The man is drinking my coffee!

tips.title: Questions start with the verb
tips.body: To ask a yes-or-no question, put the verb first: du bist müde means you are tired, and Bist du müde? means are you tired? English often adds do (do you have water?), but German simply moves the verb to the front: Hast du Wasser? With a question word like was, wer, wo, wann, wie or warum, the question word comes first and the verb comes straight after it. So Wo ist das Hotel? means where is the hotel, in the same order as English.

tips.title: Nicht and kein
tips.body: Nicht means not, so ich verstehe nicht means I don't understand. Before a noun that would have ein, or no article at all, German doesn't use nicht but says kein, which means not a or no. So ich spreche kein Deutsch means I don't speak German, and das ist kein Bier means that's not a beer. Kein takes the same endings as ein, so einen Bruder becomes keinen Bruder and eine Schwester becomes keine Schwester.

tips.title: Can, must, want: the second verb goes last
tips.body: Words like können (can), müssen (must), wollen (want) and möchten (would like) often team up with a second verb. The first verb changes with who does it, like ich kann or du kannst, and sits in its usual spot. The second verb goes to the very end of the sentence in its dictionary form, so ich möchte Wasser trinken means I would like to drink water. Everything else goes in between, and questions work the same way: Kannst du mir helfen? means can you help me? English says to drink or to help, but German needs no word for to here.

examples.en: I'd like to drink a coffee.

tips.title: Du and Sie
tips.body: German has two words for you: du for friends, family, children and people your age, and Sie for strangers, shop staff and officials. The polite Sie always has a capital S, even in the middle of a sentence. With Sie, the verb takes its dictionary form, just as it does with wir (we) and sie (they): Können Sie mir helfen? means can you help me? Sein (to be) is the exception, because you are is Sie sind. Ihr means you when you talk to several friends at once, but this app leaves its forms out.

examples.en: Excuse me, can you help me?
Can you help me? (to a friend)

tips.title: The verb comes second
tips.body: In a German statement, the verb always comes second. Second means the second part of the sentence, and a part can be one word like ich or a group of words like der Mann. You can start with the person, as in Ich gehe heute nach Hause, which means I'm going home today. If you start with something else, like a time or a place, the verb still comes second and the person moves behind it: Heute gehe ich nach Hause. So when you start with heute, morgen, jetzt or hier, put the verb next, then the person.

examples.en: Tomorrow Anna is going to Berlin.

tips.title: Verbs that split in two
tips.body: Some German verbs have a small front part that can break off: aufstehen (get up) is auf plus stehen. In an everyday sentence the front part jumps to the very end: Ich stehe früh auf means I get up early. Anrufen (call) works the same way: Ich rufe dich an means I'm calling you. In the dictionary form the verb stays in one piece, and after können or müssen it goes to the end in one piece too: Ich muss früh aufstehen. So when you hear a little word like auf or an at the end, join it back onto the verb to get the meaning.

examples.en: I have to get up early tomorrow.

tips.title: Liking: gern and mögen
tips.body: To say you like doing something, use the normal verb and put gern right after it: Ich trinke gern Kaffee means I like drinking coffee. To say you don't like doing it, put nicht before gern: Ich arbeite nicht gern means I don't like working. To like a thing or a person, use mögen, which is ich mag and du magst: Ich mag Musik means I like music. Ich möchte comes from mögen too, and it's the polite I would like, which is perfect for asking for things.

tips.title: Plurals have no single rule
tips.body: English mostly adds -s for more than one, but German plurals come in several patterns. Das Kind becomes die Kinder, die Frau becomes die Frauen, der Bruder becomes die Brüder, and das Hotel becomes die Hotels. Whether the noun is der, die or das, the word for the in the plural is always die. There's no rule you can rely on, so learn each plural together with its noun, and the answer on each card shows it to you. When you order, drinks often stay singular, so you say zwei Kaffee, bitte.

tips.title: After mit, bei and zu: the dative
tips.body: After mit (with), bei (at someone's place) and zu (to someone), the word for the or a changes, and this changed form is called the dative. Der and das become dem, die becomes der, and ein becomes einem or einer: mit dem Mann, mit der Frau, mit einem Kind. Mein changes just like ein, so you say mit meinem Vater and bei meiner Mutter. Ich becomes mir and du becomes dir, which is why you say mit mir and Wie geht es dir?

examples.target: Ich trinke Kaffee mit einem Freund.
examples.en: I'm having coffee with a friend.

examples.target: Morgen gehe ich zu meiner Mutter.
examples.en: Tomorrow I'm going to my mother's.

tips.title: Talking about the past: the Perfekt
tips.body: To talk about the past in conversation, German uses haben or sein plus a past form of the verb, and that past form goes at the end. Ich habe gearbeitet means I worked or I have worked, and ich bin nach Hause gegangen means I went home. Most verbs use haben, but verbs of moving or changing, like gehen, kommen and aufstehen, use sein. You don't have to guess which one: each verb's answer shows its past with the right helper, like hat gemacht or ist gegangen.

cards.trick: ICH sounds a bit like "itch" said softly: I have an itch, so I scratch.
SIE sounds like "zee": see her over there? She is the one you see.
DU sounds like "doo", which rhymes with "you": do you want to be my du?
ES sounds like the hissing end of "it's": it's raining, es regnet.

example.en: We're going to the cinema today.

cards.trick: WIR sounds like "veer": we veer off the road together.
ER sounds like "air": he is full of hot air.
JA sounds like "yah", just like a relaxed "yeah": it means yes.
NEIN sounds like "nine": picture a toddler shouting no nine times in a row.
BITTE sounds like BIT-uh: could you give me a bit more, please?

regional.text: Merci (Merci vielmal for thanks a lot) is very common in everyday Swiss German, alongside danke.

cards.trick: DANKE sounds like DAHN-keh, close to thank-ya: say thanks with a D and you've got it.

example.target: Möchtest du einen Kaffee? – Nein, danke.
example.en: Would you like a coffee? – No, thank you.

cards.trick: Bin sounds like English been, as in I have been here: I am.
Ist sounds like English is with a t at the end: er ist means he is.

example.target: Ich trinke Kaffee und du trinkst Tee.
example.en: I'm drinking coffee and you're drinking tea.

cards.trick: UND sounds like the start of "and" said with an oo sound: oont, and.
AUS rhymes with house: you come from the house you grew up in.

cards.target: Ich bin aus Berlin, und du?
cards.hint: informal; with sein (literally "I am"), not kommen

example.target: Ich bin aus Berlin, und du? – Ich bin aus Hamburg.
example.en: I'm from Berlin, and you? – I'm from Hamburg.

example.target: Sie ist aus Hamburg und er ist aus Berlin.
example.en: She is from Hamburg and he is from Berlin.

cards.hint: The everyday way: literally "I am called".

example.target: Ich heiße Anna und ich bin aus Berlin.
example.en: My name is Anna and I'm from Berlin.

cards.trick: Heiße is related to the old English word hight, meaning "called", as in "a knight hight Lancelot".

cards.hint: informal; the everyday way: literally "How are you called?"

example.target: Ich heiße Tom. Wie heißt du?
example.en: My name is Tom. What's your name?

cards.trick: Heißt sounds like the old English word hight, which meant "named", as in "a knight hight Lancelot".

cards.hint: The short two-word reply, not schön, dich kennenzulernen

example.target: Freut mich! Ich bin aus Hamburg.
example.en: Nice to meet you! I'm from Hamburg.

cards.hint: The two-word reply to thanks, not bitte

example.target: Nein, ich bin nicht aus Hamburg.

cards.trick: NICHT sounds a bit like nix, the slang word for no or nothing: nicht means not.
GUT sounds like "goot", almost exactly the English word "good", and it means good.

example.target: Ich heiße Anna. Freut mich sehr!
example.en: I'm Anna. Very nice to meet you!

cards.trick: SEHR sounds like "zair", like a zebra's hair: very, very stripy.

cards.hint: the everyday greeting, not guten Tag
cards.trick: HALLO sounds like HAH-low, almost hello, and that is just what it means.

example.target: Ich bin sehr müde, und du?

cards.trick: MÜDE sounds a bit like moody: when you're tired, you get moody.
Think of the old English "How goes it?": geht means goes, and 's is short for es, it.

example.target: Wie geht's? – Mir geht's gut, danke.
example.en: How are you? – I'm fine, thanks.

cards.trick: Think of it word for word as "me it goes good": mir sounds like "me", and gut sounds like "good".

cards.hint: informal, asking back how someone is

example.target: Mir geht's gut, danke. Und dir?
Hallo! Wie geht's? – Gut, danke. Und dir?
example.en: Hello! How are you? – Fine, thanks. And you?

cards.trick: Wieder means again and sehen means see, so it is literally until we see each other again.

example.target: Wie geht's? – Ich bin sehr müde.
example.en: How are you? – I'm very tired.

cards.trick: Habe (HAH-buh) is just English have with a b in place of the v.
Du hast is old English thou hast, meaning you have.
Er hat sounds close to hat: he has a hat.
EIN rhymes with "mine": think "a mine", and ein is simply a or an.

cards.hint: polite wish, the modal verb möchten, not hätte gern

example.target: Sie hat ein Haus, ich nicht.
example.en: She has a house, I don't.

cards.trick: HAUS sounds almost exactly like house, and that's what it means.
WASSER sounds like VAH-ser, a close cousin of English water, with the W said as a V.
KAFFEE sounds like "café", the place where you go to drink coffee.

example.target: Er hat ein Haus mit Garten.
example.en: He has a house with a garden.

example.target: Hallo! Ich möchte ein Wasser, bitte.
example.en: Hello! I'd like a water, please.

cards.trick: DER sounds like "dare": I dare the man to drink the coffee.
MEIN sounds just like English "mine", and it means my.
MANN sounds just like the English word man, and that is exactly what it means.
FRAU rhymes with wow: wow, look at that woman!
KIND, said like kint, is the kinder in kindergarten, literally a garden for children.
VATER is said FAH-ter, because German v sounds like f, so it sounds almost exactly like father.
MUTTER, said MUT-ter as in mutt, is close to MOTHER: picture a mother hugging her mutt.
BRUDER sounds like brooder, and your brother broods over everything at the family dinner.
SCHWESTER sounds like "shvester", close to "sister" with a swish, as if your sister stole your sweater.

example.target: Hallo! Das ist meine Mutter, Anna.
example.en: Hello! This is my mother, Anna.

example.target: Mein Bruder ist aus Hamburg, und ich bin aus Berlin.
example.en: My brother is from Hamburg, and I'm from Berlin.

cards.trick: ESSEN starts with the sound of the letter S: picture yourself eating a big S-shaped pretzel.
TRINKEN sounds like "drinking": you drink when you trinkst.
BIER sounds like "beer" because it means beer.
TEE sounds like "tay", which is close to "tea": a cup of Tee is a cup of tea.

example.target: Meine Mutter hat den Mann gern.
Ich habe meinen Vater sehr gern.

cards.trick: mein takes the same ending as ein: einen Bruder, meinen Vater.

example.target: Ich habe einen Bruder und eine Schwester.
example.en: I have a brother and a sister.

example.target: Ich habe eine Schwester und einen Bruder.
example.en: I have a sister and a brother.

cards.hint: the object of an unspoken ich möchte (I'd like)

example.target: Ich trinke den Tee, nicht den Kaffee.
example.en: I'm drinking the tea, not the coffee.

cards.target: Ich habe einen Bruder und eine Schwester.
cards.en: I have a brother and a sister.

example.target: Ich habe einen Bruder und eine Schwester. Und du?
example.en: I have a brother and a sister. And you?

cards.target: Einen Kaffee und ein Bier, bitte.
cards.en: A coffee and a beer, please.

example.target: Hallo! Ich möchte einen Kaffee und ein Bier, bitte.
example.en: Hello! I'd like a coffee and a beer, please.

cards.trick: WAS sounds like "vass", close to "what's": what's that? Was ist das?
WIE sounds like vee: picture someone shrugging with arms in a V shape, asking how?
WO sounds like "voh", as in "voilà": you say it while pointing at where something is.
cards.why: Use wo for where something is; woher for where someone comes from.

cards.trick: WARUM sounds like vah-ROOM: why does that car keep going vah-room outside my window?
WER, said like vair, sounds close to where, but it asks who; the German for where is wo.
cards.why: Wer asks who, even though it sounds like where; for where, use wo.

example.en: When do you want to eat?

cards.trick: WANN sounds like "van": when does the van come?

cards.hint: from where, not wo or wohin
cards.trick: WOHER sounds like 'vo-hair': where did that hair come from?
cards.why: Use woher to ask where someone or something comes from; wo asks where something is.

example.target: Was ist das? – Das ist Tee.
Wer ist er? – Das ist mein Bruder.
example.en: Who is he? – That's my brother.

cards.trick: Weiß sounds like vice, close to wise, and a wise person knows things.

example.en: Do you know where he is?

cards.trick: Weißt sounds like vicet, almost wised: you got wise, so you know.

example.target: Er weiß, wo meine Mutter ist.
example.en: He knows where my mother is.

cards.trick: Weiß sounds like vice, close to wise, and a wise person knows things.
KEIN sounds like "kine", rhyming with nein, the German no: kein means no or not a.
cards.why: Use kein before a noun that would take ein or no article; use nicht to say not anywhere else.

cards.trick: verSTEHEN sounds like "fair SHTAY-en": if you stay and listen fairly, you'll understand.
SPRECHEN sounds a bit like SPEECH-en: when you speak, you make speech.

cards.hint: adjective, as in German beer; not the language or a person
cards.trick: DEUTSCH sounds like "DOYTCH", close to "Dutch": Pennsylvania Dutch settlers were really Germans.

example.target: Ich habe keinen Bruder und keine Schwester.
example.en: I have no brother and no sister.

example.target: Ich habe keine Schwester, ich habe einen Bruder.
example.en: I don't have a sister, I have a brother.

example.target: Ich verstehe nicht. Sprechen Sie Englisch?
example.en: I don't understand. Do you speak English?

cards.trick: Verstehen has stehen, to stand, inside it, just as understand has stand.
Einmal starts with ein, meaning one, so noch einmal is literally still one time.

cards.en: How do you say … in German?

example.target: Wie sagt man das auf Deutsch?
example.en: How do you say that in German?

example.target: Ich verstehe das nicht, ich spreche kein Deutsch.
example.en: I don't understand that, I don't speak German.

example.target: Hallo, sprechen Sie Englisch? Ich spreche kein Deutsch.
example.en: Hello, do you speak English? I don't speak German.

cards.trick: Kann sounds almost exactly like English can, and means the same thing.
Kannst is like old English thou canst: can plus the st ending that du forms take.

example.target: Meine Mutter kann sehr gut Englisch sprechen.
example.en: My mother can speak English very well.

cards.trick: Same as ich: kann sounds like can, with no ending for he or she, just like English.

example.target: Kannst du mir das noch einmal sagen?
example.en: Can you say that to me again?

cards.trick: MIR sounds like the start of mirror: look in a mirror and you see me.
cards.why: Use mir for to me and after helfen or mit; use mich when me is the direct object.
